guidance: Give the visual subject the strongest contrast. Put contextual boundaries, grids, and secondary places lower in the visual hierarchy. Verify at the size the audience will actually see.
example: For a report about three affected counties, use one prominent fill for the counties and quieter outlines for their neighbours. Start the reader at the headline and the evidence.

guidance: Use the title and a small number of annotations to direct attention, while preserving enough surrounding context to let readers inspect the evidence. Only state conclusions supported by the supplied data.
example: Use a regional locator when local geography is unfamiliar. Use a descriptive annotation for a documented change, and leave out a causal claim that the inputs cannot support.

guidance: Match the ramp to the structure of the data. Use ordered lightness for magnitudes and a justified midpoint for diverging values. Give missing observations their own treatment and keep true zeros in the data scale.
example: A map of values above and below a policy target can diverge around the documented target. A map of positive access rates uses an ordered scale.

guidance: Use rates or normalized values where appropriate for area fill. Show comparable raw totals with symbols sized by area. Derive a rate only if the numerator and denominator describe the same place, period, and population.
example: County unemployment totals and county unemployment rates are different stories. Use an area fill for the documented rate and sized symbols for totals.

guidance: Use symbol area for quantity, preserve a visible outline where marks overlap, and label the places central to the story first. Treat site coordinates and estimated centroids as different kinds of evidence.
example: Show a hospital network as sites only when locations are verified. County-wide totals use regional symbols with a legend explaining their placement.

guidance: Keep the source, elevation units, and orientation legible in the flat panel. Use hillshade to reveal landforms without letting shadows overpower elevation colours.
example: Pair a restrained elevation ramp and north-up plan with a separate oblique image. Readers can locate forms on the plan and understand their shape in the scene.

guidance: An orthographic view provides a useful alternative when perspective draws too much attention to the foreground. Select an angle that exposes the landforms relevant to the brief, and disclose any vertical exaggeration.
example: Compare a lower view that emphasizes ridgelines with a higher view that reveals valley connections. Use a higher view when foreground terrain hides the relationship under discussion.
